segs.cue: you've already introduced yourself; start straight on the cover

segs.t: So my project is called Poise. It helps you notice when your posture drifts, without breaking your focus. I made a web app and a light bar that sits on your monitor.

I picked this project for two reasons. First, it shows the whole process, from research to design, testing and iteration, so you can see what I changed at each step. Second, I used AI all the way through, so I can show you how it helped me make decisions.
So, let me walk you through it.
First, the problem and my research. Then version one, what I changed, and version two. And last, what I learned using AI.

segs.cue: quick: one short line per press

segs.t: This is how I define the problem in one sentence. We drift without noticing.
At first, we sit up straight.
Then sometimes, we rest our chin on our hand.
Bit by bit, we lean in closer to the screen.
Over time, the neck and lower back start to hurt.
And fixing it later can cost thousands. I've had neck and back pain myself, and spent a lot on physical therapy and a good chair. And I wasn't the only one.

So I looked at some research to see if other people feel the same. The average US adult sits about six hours a day. Up to 63 percent of office workers get neck pain in a year. And back and neck pain is the biggest health cost in the US, about 135 billion dollars.
So yeah, it's not just me.
Then I ran a quick survey with fifteen people.

Three things stood out. Nine out of fifteen rarely notice their posture, or only once it hurts. Fourteen feel pain after a long session, mostly in the neck and lower back. And most of what they'd tried, like stretching or a better chair, comes after. So nothing really catches it early.
To go deeper, I interviewed three of them, Paul, Hyunjoo and Peter.
So, Paul only notices he's slouching when his lower back starts to hurt.
Hyunjoo bought a Herman Miller chair. It helped at first, but sitting straight for long was still hard.
And Peter leans toward the screen when he focuses. He works in quiet places, so a silent reminder would help him.
So I found an opportunity for each of them.
For Paul, I can help him notice earlier.
For Hyunjoo, I can give him short breaks to reset and sit well again.
And for Peter, I can give him a signal that doesn't interrupt him.

Next I looked at what's already out there. Posture apps notice early and the cue is clear, but they buzz or pop up and interrupt your work. And chairs and Pilates are things people try after it already hurts.

I also like seeing what I can bring in from other services. Like when I order on DoorDash, I can see my order on the lock screen without opening the app. Uber, Starbucks and Nike Run Club work in a similar way.

So I noticed a gap. Posture apps and tools either interrupt you or come after it already hurts, so I saw a chance for something in between. And since these apps all show live status on the lock screen without opening the app, I could show people their posture live.
So from all three, I needed to help people notice early, with a clear cue that doesn't interrupt them.
So I thought, if people get a clear cue that helps them notice early, with no interruptions, they'll catch the drift sooner and stay aligned longer.

So for the user, I wanted the app to tell you when you drift and the light bar to change color as you move, so you notice it without stopping your work. And for the business, I'd keep the app free so people can try it first, then offer the light bar. Seeing their posture get better over time would turn it into a daily habit.
Here's how it works in five steps.
First, you answer four questions, pick the camera or the sensor, and plug in the light bar.
Then you start working. The app checks your posture and the light stays white.
If you drift, the app shows what changed and the light turns yellow, then red. When you sit back up, it turns green and fades back to white.
When you finish, a report shows how long you sat well.
Then you take a break with stretches or a game, and the light plays along.

segs.cue: the recording plays; press once per part

segs.t: So here's what it looks like, in four parts.

First, onboarding. Poise asks four questions, like how long you focus, how it should tell you when you drift, what helps you rest, and if breaks should start on their own. I came up with this from the interviews, because everyone worked differently, so setup starts from your own answers.

Next is focus mode. The bar on the right fills up as you drift, and the label tells you how you moved. And the light bar turns yellow, then red, and green when you sit back up. And at the end, a report shows how long you stayed aligned.
I came up with this from the survey, because nine out of fifteen only noticed once it hurt, so the bar reacts right away.
Then break mode. This figure shows you each stretch, and the camera checks how closely you match it as a percent. Up top, you can switch to a reset or a small game.
I came up with this from the survey too, because a lot of people stretch to fix their posture, so I made this break mode to help them reset.
And last, settings. In this modal, you can change your modes, how bright the light bar glows, and the music.
I came up with this from the interviews, because everyone has different preferences, so there are a few options to choose from.
This is also part of my school project, so I showed my app and the light bar to my classmates, and I mostly watched and took notes.
And watching people use it changed what I thought mattered.
On the good side, people loved having options for a break and being able to shut off the camera. So they liked having control.

But from the light alone, they couldn't tell how they moved. Twelve guide steps felt like too much, and some worried what the camera collects. So setup was slow and the light wasn't clear. And people wanted to feel safe with the camera.
And for new ideas, they wanted to just type the mode they want, and keep a small window open while they work. So they wanted it their own way, and always in view.
So I planned the next version from two places.

From my classmates, the biggest one was privacy. The app already said the camera never records, but it was too small, so people missed it. So I'll make that clearer and explain the sensor. The trade off is, the sensor is less accurate than the camera.
Next, clearer cues. I thought the light bar was enough, but it wasn't, so when you drift, a voice tells you how to fix it. The trade off is, a voice can interrupt you.
And people wanted it simpler and more their own. So I'll add a text bar called Ask Poise to change settings, a mini window and a shorter guide. The trade off is, more features, more to learn.
From my own review, I'll add a figure that moves with you, and keep the number. The trade off is, the figure is less exact, and the number is smaller.
I'll use one design system, since version one looked uneven. The trade off is, edge cases need new rules and can limit creativity.
And I'll take the green out, since going back to white already shows you're sitting well. The trade off is, sitting up feels a little less rewarded.

So I built version two with the same five steps, and you can see what I changed in green. Set up has a clearer camera or sensor choice. Focus adds a figure and a mini window. And when you drift, a voice tells you how to fix it, and the light goes yellow, red, and back to white. In the report, you can hover the chart for each moment. And in the break, the same figure now shows up in every game.

segs.cue: the recording plays; press once per change

segs.t: So here's version two. There are six changes, so I'll go quickly.

First, camera or sensor. So now, before you start, Poise tells you how each one works. The camera never records you, and the sensor just checks how far you sit from the screen. I came up with this from the playtest, because people were worried about the camera, and didn't really know what the sensor was for.

Next, simpler steps. I grouped the twelve guide steps by topic into four, so each one is easier to understand. And changing a mode is now a short side panel, not a long list of sliders. I came up with this from the playtest, because twelve steps was too much before even starting.

Then, easier to notice. A figure moves with you, the card changes color as you drift, and a voice tells you how to fix it. And in the report, you can hover the chart to see what moved. I came up with this from the playtest, because people wanted to know what to fix, not just a light.

This is the mini window. You can use Poise in a small window over your other tabs, so you keep tracking while you work. I came up with this from the playtest, because people wanted something small to keep open while they work.

And this is Ask Poise. I added a text field where you can just type what you want, like a one hour focus with breathing breaks, and Poise sets it up for you. I came up with this from the playtest, because people had a hard time finding settings, and wanted it their own way.

And last, one look and feel. To make it feel more polished, I carefully adjusted the typography, color and spacing, and set rules for each, so it all became one design system. I came up with this from my own review, because version one looked uneven in color, typography and spacing, so now it feels like one product.
Then I tested version two with Paul, Hyunjoo and Peter at their own desks, for an hour each.
Overall, people liked the small changes, like the figure that follows you and the little window. So it helped without breaking focus.
But when Peter was on a call, the voice told him to sit up in the middle of it, and he had to leave the little window just to take a break. So it got in the way of calls and breaks.
And there were some new ideas, like having the voice go quiet during meetings, or seeing when they slouch the most each week. So people want it to fit their day and habits.
Then I measured it, with the same three people, and they did the same things in version one and version two.

The one I cared about most was time aligned, because my hypothesis was that people would catch the drift sooner and stay aligned longer. It went from 85 to 90 percent. That might sound small, but everyone already sat well most of the time. All three went up, and Peter, who drifted the most, improved the most.
So they stayed aligned longer, and it got easier to use.
Now, what I learned using AI, since I used it at almost every step.

In research, I only had one month, and I wanted to spend most of it talking to people and hearing their stories. So AI found papers and drafted my questions. But I read each paper myself and organized the questions. So AI finds and drafts fast, but judging what fits is still my job.

When building, I wanted a real app to test within days, so AI coded the app and the Arduino from my flow. Then I had people try each build and watched them drift. So AI lets me build real things, but only users can tell if they work.

And for testing, AI handled the quantitative data. It turned every session into numbers and compared version one and two. But I still checked every number myself against each session. And because AI did the counting, I could focus on the qualitative side, watching people use a real app, not a mockup, and catching things numbers can't show, like when the voice cut into Peter's call. So AI shows me what happened, but watching people shows me why.
So yeah, AI made me a lot faster, but what I'm most proud of is that every change came from watching real people use it.
That's Poise. Thanks so much for listening. You can try it yourself with the link below, and I'd love to hear any questions you have.
